specPoints.text: understand the terms: i rate of reaction ii rate equation, rate= k [A] m [B] n where m and n are 0, 1 or 2 iii order with respect to a substance in a rate equation iv overall order of a reaction v rate constant vi half-life vii rate-determining step viii activation energy ix heterogeneous and homogeneous catalyst

primer.text: Rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are consumed or products formed, in mol dm-3 s-1. This note defines rate, shows how concentration data reveal a proportional relationship between rate and concentration, and introduces the rate equation, where experimentally determined orders and a rate constant tie reactant concentrations to rate. Products and catalysts may appear; intermediates never do.

lessons.title: Defining the rate of reaction
lessons.opening: Kinetics begins with a definition: the rate of reaction is how quickly a reactant is consumed or a product appears, per unit time. This lesson fixes the units, lists the physical changes a chemist can watch to follow a reaction, and sets up the model reaction used throughout the topic.
keyPoints: Rate of reaction tracks how fast a reactant is used up or a product forms, expressed as a concentration change per unit time with units mol dm-3 s-1.
Rate can be followed by measuring mass lost, gas volume produced, colour or pH change, or electrical conductivity as time passes.
Rate is calculated as concentration change divided by the time interval over which that change happens.
The model reaction D (aq) to E (aq) plus F (g) lets rates be tabulated at several concentrations of D.

low.restatement: Rate is a concentration change divided by time, tracked through any property that moves with concentration such as mass, volume, colour, pH or conductivity.
low.analogy: A bathroom scale tells you how fast a bathtub drains only if you weigh it every few seconds; each weighing is one rate data point.
low.examPointer: Quote the units mol dm-3 s-1 whenever you state a rate - examiners check them.

medium.restatement: Because rate compares two quantities, concentration and time, any measurable stand-in for concentration works; the property only needs to change smoothly as the reaction proceeds.
medium.analogy: Watching a kettle cool: you cannot read temperature directly, but the steam thins, the glass mist fades and the sound softens - each is a proxy for the falling temperature.
medium.examPointer: If asked how to follow a given reaction, pick the property that changes and justify the choice from the state symbols.

check.stem: What are the units of rate of reaction when concentration is tracked?

options.text: mol dm-3 s-1
options.explanation: Rate is a concentration change per time, so concentration units divide by seconds.

options.text: mol dm-3
options.explanation: That is a concentration, not a change in concentration over time.
That would suit a first-order rate constant, not a rate measured in concentration terms.

options.text: g s-1
options.explanation: Mass-based rates are possible experimentally, but the defined rate unit here is concentration per time.

check.stem: Which property change could NOT follow the course of the reaction D (aq) to E (aq) plus F (g)?

options.text: A fall in the volume of D present in the mixture
options.explanation: D is aqueous and its concentration changes as it reacts, so tracking it is sensible.

options.text: The mass of the reaction vessel and contents
options.explanation: Mass follows the escape of gaseous F, so it changes measurably.

options.text: A colour change as E accumulates
options.explanation: Colour tracks concentration whenever the mixture changes appearance.

options.text: A constant electrical conductivity reading
options.explanation: Conductivity only carries rate information when ion concentrations change; here it stays constant, so it cannot follow the course.

check.stem: Rate of reaction is calculated by dividing

options.text: The change in concentration of a reactant or product by the time taken for that change
options.explanation: The definition is concentration change per unit time.

options.text: The total volume of product by the total mass of reactant
options.explanation: Neither ratio carries time, so neither is a rate.

options.text: The time taken by the temperature rise
options.explanation: Temperature is not the defined quantity here and the ratio is inverted.

options.text: The concentration of product by the concentration of reactant
options.explanation: That compares two concentrations at one instant, not a change over time.

check.stem: Gas volume collected over time is a valid rate measurement because

options.text: The volume of gas produced is proportional to the amount of product formed
options.explanation: Gas moles map directly onto product amount through the equation.

options.text: Gas volume always equals the volume of solution used
options.explanation: There is no such equality in rate work.

options.text: Gases dissolve completely in the solution
options.explanation: Collected gases are assumed not to dissolve significantly.

options.text: Volume is independent of the reaction
options.explanation: The whole point is that gas volume grows as reaction proceeds.

check.stem: A student measures the mass of a flask at 10-second intervals as carbon dioxide escapes. The mass readings give rate information because

options.text: The falling mass measures reactant or mixture amount at each instant, so differences between readings measure change over time
options.explanation: Successive mass readings give concentration-equivalent changes over measured intervals.

options.text: Mass and volume are identical quantities
options.explanation: They are distinct physical quantities.

options.text: The balance itself changes the rate
options.explanation: Weighing does not alter the reaction.

options.text: Mass loss equals rate directly without any calculation
options.explanation: A mass reading is an amount, not a rate; rate needs the change divided by time.

check.stem: State the definition of rate of reaction and its units.
check.modelAnswer: Rate of reaction is the concentration change of a chosen reactant or product divided by the time interval, recorded in mol dm-3 s-1.

check.stem: List three measurable changes that can be used to follow the rate of a reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Any three of: mass lost over time, volume of gas produced, colour change or colorimetry, pH change, or electrical conductivity change.

check.stem: Explain why the model reaction D (aq) to E (aq) plus F (g) is convenient for studying rate at different concentrations of D.
check.modelAnswer: The gaseous product F can be collected so its volume tracks progress directly, while D stays in solution where samples of known concentration can be prepared, so rates at several starting concentrations of D can be measured and tabulated side by side.

check.stem: A reaction liberates hydrogen gas, but a student proposes monitoring it by colour change. Comment on the suitability and suggest a better measurement.
check.modelAnswer: Hydrogen and its solutions are colourless, so no colour signal develops and colorimetry would read a flat line; collecting the hydrogen volume in a gas syringe instead gives a directly proportional measure of product formed against time.

lessons.title: From concentration data to the rate equation
lessons.opening: Tabulated rates for the model reaction show rate rising in step with the concentration of D. That proportionality condenses into the rate expression rate = k[D], and the general rate equation rate = k[A]^m[B]^n follows. This lesson separates what rate equations may contain from what they may not.
keyPoints: The tabulated data for D show rate and concentration rising together, a directly proportional relationship.
Proportionality is written as the rate expression rate proportional to [D], or rate = k[D], where k is the rate constant.
For A plus B giving C plus D the general rate equation is rate = k[A]^m[B]^n with orders m and n.
Orders must be found by experiment; stoichiometric coefficients never fix them.
Products and catalysts may appear in a rate equation, but intermediates do not.

low.restatement: Doubling [D] doubles the rate, so rate = k[D]; in general rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, with the powers found only from experiments.
low.analogy: A volume dial on a hose: turn it twice as far and twice as much water flows - the dial setting and flow are proportional, like [D] and rate here.
low.examPointer: State plainly that rate equations come from experiment, never from the balancing numbers.

medium.restatement: The rate constant k is the proportionality glue between concentration and rate; the powers m and n are the orders that experiments reveal, not the balancing numbers that the equation happens to carry.
medium.analogy: A recipe that scales: the serving count scales with ingredients (the proportional part), but only tasting the dish tells you which ingredient dominates the flavour (the experimental orders).
medium.examPointer: If an option claims orders can be read from the stoichiometric equation, reject it outright - that is the classic trap.

check.stem: The data for D show that doubling [D] doubles the rate. The rate expression is therefore

options.text: rate = k[D], first order in D
options.explanation: Direct proportionality means a power of one on [D].

options.text: rate = k[D]2, second order in D
options.explanation: Squaring would make doubling concentration quadruple the rate.

options.text: rate = k, zero order in D
options.explanation: Zero order would leave rate unchanged as [D] moves.

options.text: rate = k[D] raised to a fractional power
options.explanation: Fractional orders exist but this clean doubling shows power one.

check.stem: In the rate equation rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, the values of m and n

options.text: Must be determined experimentally
options.explanation: Orders are kinetic facts that only measurement reveals.

options.text: Equal the balancing coefficients of A and B
options.explanation: Stoichiometry does not fix orders.

options.text: Are always 1 and 1
options.explanation: Orders take zero, positive and sometimes fractional values.

options.text: Are fixed by the temperature
options.explanation: Temperature changes k, not the orders.

check.stem: Which species may legitimately appear in a rate equation?

options.text: A catalyst used in the reaction
options.explanation: Catalysts can feature because they affect the rate-determining chemistry.

options.text: Any intermediate formed and consumed en route
options.explanation: Intermediates are excluded from rate equations.

options.text: Only gaseous reactants
options.explanation: Rate equations include whatever the mechanism involves, whatever its state.

options.text: Every species in the stoichiometric equation
options.explanation: Being in the overall equation does not guarantee a rate role.

check.stem: The rate constant k in rate = k[D] is best described as

options.text: The proportionality constant connecting rate to the concentrations raised to their powers
options.explanation: k glues the concentration terms to the rate.

options.text: A second rate measured in different units
options.explanation: k is not itself a rate.

options.text: A quantity that rises when more D is added
options.explanation: Changing concentration moves along the expression; k is unchanged.

options.text: A fixed universal constant for all reactions
options.explanation: k is characteristic of each reaction and changes with temperature.

check.stem: Rate equations can only be determined experimentally because

options.text: The orders describe mechanism behaviour that the stoichiometric equation does not encode
options.explanation: Balancing numbers say nothing about the slow-step chemistry that sets orders.

options.text: Concentrations cannot be measured
options.explanation: Concentrations are routinely measured in kinetics work.

options.text: k changes during every experiment
options.explanation: k stays constant at fixed temperature.

options.text: Rate equations change during a run
options.explanation: The rate equation is fixed for a given reaction and temperature.

check.stem: State the rate expression for the reaction where rate is proportional to [D].
check.modelAnswer: Rate = k[D], with k the rate constant and the reaction first order with respect to D.

check.stem: Write the general rate equation for A plus B giving C plus D, naming each symbol.
check.modelAnswer: Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where k is the rate constant, [A] and [B] are reactant concentrations, and m and n are the orders with respect to A and B.

check.stem: Explain why an intermediate does not feature in a rate equation even though it takes part in the chemistry.
check.modelAnswer: An intermediate is made and consumed inside the mechanism rather than supplied by the chemist, so its concentration is not an independent variable; the rate equation is expressed in terms of what is actually added and controlled, which is why intermediates are absent.

check.stem: A reaction's stoichiometric equation shows 2A plus B forming products, yet experiment gives rate = k[A]. Reconcile the two statements.
check.modelAnswer: The balancing numbers and the kinetic orders are independent: the experiment shows the rate depends only on one power of A, so the slow chemistry involves A but not free B; the coefficient 2 in the overall equation is bookkeeping, not an order, and the rate equation from experiment stands.

glossary.definition: How quickly a reactant is used up or a product forms, expressed as a concentration change per unit time, in mol dm-3 s-1.
The expression rate = k[A]^m[B]^n linking rate to reactant concentrations raised to experimentally determined powers.
The proportionality factor k in a rate equation, fixed for a given reaction at a given temperature.
A species made and consumed within a mechanism that never appears in the rate equation.
